title: MVP: The Smallest Ethical Test of Value
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: MVP: The Smallest Ethical Test of Value.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Before choosing a format, state what must be learned. A useful contract contains five parts:

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at begin with a learning contract?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: 1. Person and situation: who has the problem, in what context, and what progress are they trying to make? 2. Value hypothesis: what change do we believe our intervention will create for them? 3. Riskiest assumption: what would make the whole idea untrue, harmful, or commercially unworkable? 4.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Evidence threshold: what observation would strengthen, weaken, or invalidate the hypothesis? 5. Non-negotiable boundaries: what must not be compromised while learning—safety, accessibility, privacy, informed consent, legal duties, trust, or recoverability?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Without this contract, “MVP” becomes an argument for scope reduction rather than learning. A thin feature can produce a high click-through rate while teaching nothing about whether it solves a meaningful problem.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Match the test to the uncertainty
turns.text: What changes when we look at match the test to the uncertainty?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The smallest useful test depends on the question. Use a sketch, scenario, or interview when you need to learn whether a problem is real and important. Use a concept prototype when you need to learn whether the proposed value makes sense. Use a task prototype when you need to learn whether people can operate an interaction.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use a concierge or Wizard-of-Oz service when the experience requires human judgement but the automated system is not ready. Use a limited real release only when the value, usability, operational capacity, and safeguards are sufficiently understood.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The format is not a maturity ladder. A manual service may be the most honest way to learn whether people value a result before investing in automation. A high-fidelity prototype may be necessary when the risk lies in timing, trust, or complex interaction. The test is “minimum” only if removing more would make the evidence misleading.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at viability includes quality boundaries?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The word viable has three dimensions. The experience must plausibly create value for a person; the organisation must be able to sustain or learn from it; and the intervention must be safe enough for the context in which it is offered. Accessibility, privacy, clear communication, and recovery are not enhancements to defer until scale.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: They determine whether the evidence comes from a representative group and whether people can participate without unjustifiable burden.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: For a financial-advice concept, an ethical early test might explicitly position the output as educational, keep the recommendation narrowly scoped, show uncertainty, provide a route to qualified help, avoid acting automatically on behalf of a customer, and recruit only people for whom that limited experience is appropriate.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team should be able to explain what the system cannot do as clearly as what it can.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at decide before the result arrives?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Precommit to the decision logic. Write down what would lead to iteration, expansion, a different hypothesis, or withdrawal. Include guardrails as well as success signals. A test may meet its engagement target and still stop if it creates confusion, unequal access, excessive support demand, privacy concerns, or a consequence the team did not anticipate.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: This discipline prevents post-hoc storytelling. If the team only decides what counts after seeing a result, every outcome can be rationalised as progress. Lean learning works when a result can genuinely change the next action.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Minimum scope must preserve the causal mechanism
turns.text: What changes when we look at minimum scope must preserve the causal mechanism?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Remove features that do not affect the learning question, but retain the chain needed to produce the outcome. A prototype of a provider form can test comprehension; it cannot test whether routing reaches the correct owner or whether fresher information prevents patient failure.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A concierge can test service value, but manual expertise and response time must be included when interpreting scalability.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Name what is real, simulated, omitted, and supported manually. Otherwise stakeholders compare pilot performance with a future system that lacks the very humans who made it work.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at recruit and expose proportionately?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: An early test should involve people for whom the boundaries and fallback are appropriate. Do not target those with the least power to refuse simply because recruitment is easy. Use staged exposure, informed participation where research is involved, monitoring, stop authority, and support proportional to consequence.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Some product releases are experiments on behaviour even when not labelled research. Ethical responsibility does not disappear because the feature is called beta. Clarify limitations without transferring risk to users through a blanket disclaimer.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: cash-flow guidance?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A small-business tool wants to test automated cash-flow recommendations. The smallest ethical test may be a reviewed educational scenario with historical or synthetic data, clear uncertainty, no automatic movement of funds, and access to a qualified route. A live lightly tested score with authoritative language is small in functionality but large in consequence.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Feature-minimum instead of evidence-minimum. The team removes functionality but keeps a test that cannot answer the important question.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Fake certainty. A prototype or manual service presents itself as a mature automated capability, so participants make decisions on a false basis.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Unprotected experimentation. The organisation learns by shifting the cost of uncertainty to people with fewer choices or less ability to recover.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Metric theatre. A vanity signal such as sign-ups is treated as proof of value while the intended outcome remains unmeasured.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No operational reality. A promising prototype is tested without the support, data, policy, or staffing conditions needed for a live service, then interpreted as launch readiness.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Manual magic. Concierge staff silently supply data, judgement, and recovery that the proposed scaled system will not have.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Beta disclaimer: an early label is used to shift responsibility for foreseeable harm onto participants.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Unrepresentative convenience: only easy-to-serve users or partners are included, so feasibility and access look stronger than they are.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: When someone says “we can fix that after launch,” ask who will carry the consequence before the fix exists. If the answer is the person using the product, the scope may be small but the experiment is not ethically small.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Senior practitioners protect the possibility of a negative result. They prevent roadmap or investor commitments from making every outcome look like validation, distinguish manual pilot capability from scalable capability, and require stop authority close to the observed harm.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: They know that a smaller population does not justify lower integrity when individual consequence remains high.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A team wants to offer instant cash-flow advice to small businesses. To move quickly, it calls a lightly tested scoring model an MVP, gives it authoritative language, and releases it to customers who use it to decide whether they can pay suppliers. The scope is small, but the consequence is not.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A feature can be minimum without being viable; it can be viable for the organisation while exposing customers to risk they cannot see. An MVP is not a synonym for an unfinished product. It is the smallest responsible intervention that can test a meaningful value hypothesis.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: lesson 197 connected discovery and delivery. This lesson chooses the next learning increment inside that rhythm. lesson 199 will distinguish the different questions an MVP can answer so that a usable interaction is not mistaken for a validated opportunity.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose one planned feature. Write the five-part learning contract. Then design two possible tests: the cheapest test and the smallest test that would produce valid, ethically acceptable evidence. Compare what each fails to reveal.
